title: CGT 50% discount replaced by indexation and a 30% minimum tax
headline: Gains made after 1 July 2027 lose the 50% CGT discount: the cost base is indexed to inflation and individuals pay at least 30%. Earlier gains keep the discount.
summary: Individuals and trusts lose the 50% CGT discount for growth after 30 June 2027. Instead the cost base is indexed to inflation, and individuals pay at least 30% tax on those gains. Assets held at 30 June 2027 are split at their market value just before 1 July 2027: growth up to then keeps the 50% discount. It covers property, shares, ETFs, crypto and other CGT assets. The main residence exemption is unchanged.
effectiveLabel: CGT events on or after 1 July 2027

history.note: Senate passed with 30 Government and 3 Greens amendments; House agreed

bigStat.caption: minimum tax on capital gains made after 1 July 2027

before: Individuals and trusts that held an asset for more than 12 months paid tax on only 50% of the capital gain.
The discount applied to the whole gain, however long the asset was held.
after: Growth after 1 July 2027: the cost base is indexed to inflation (quarterly CPI) instead of halving the gain.
Individuals pay at least 30% on those post-2027 gains, unless they receive income support such as the Age Pension or JobSeeker during the year.
Growth up to 1 July 2027 keeps the 50% discount. It is measured using market value just before 1 July 2027; an optional apportioning method is still in draft.
Qualifying new residential builds can keep the 50% discount instead, and then the minimum tax does not apply.
exemptions: Your main residence: the exemption is unchanged.
Gains that accrued before 1 July 2027 keep the 50% discount.
Companies and super funds are outside the change; complying super funds keep their one-third discount.
Qualifying new residential dwellings can keep the 50% discount and stay out of the minimum tax.
Individuals receiving income support payments during the year are exempt from the 30% minimum tax.

workedExample.title: Budget example: Jane's investment property
steps: Bought 1 July 2022 for $800,000. Worth $1,131,371 at 1 July 2027. Sold 1 July 2032 for $1.6 million. Inflation 2.5% a year.
Growth to 1 July 2027 is $331,371. The 50% discount leaves $165,685 taxable.
Growth after: $1,600,000 less the indexed value of $1,280,042 leaves $319,958 taxable.
Total taxable gain: $485,643, against $400,000 if the 50% discount still applied.
workedExample.result: At a 47% marginal rate including Medicare levy, tax of $228,252 instead of $188,000.

actions.text: Keep records of every purchase, cost and capital improvement with its date: indexation is worked out item by item, by quarter.
Don't get a valuation dated before 1 July 2027. The ATO says the value needed is market value immediately before that date, and only when you sell.
For listed shares and ETFs, record the quoted price at 30 June 2027.
Keep evidence for both a valuation and the apportioning method: you choose when you lodge the return for the year you sell.
Model future sales with indexation and the 30% minimum, especially if your income will be low when you sell, such as in retirement.

positions.summary: Legislated the change, describing it as returning capital gains tax to its original intent from 1 July 2027.
Will "reverse Labor's changes to capital gains tax". Angus Taylor: a Coalition government he leads will repeal them. No repeal date or transition rules given.
Voted for the law after amendments removed a Treasurer power to extend the 50% discount. Want concessions ended rather than grandfathered.
Completely opposes the CGT changes and would restore the 50% discount if elected.
Back the housing reform but want business assets and shares treated differently. Allegra Spender proposes a flat 40% discount for active assets while keeping the 30% minimum.

caveats: The optional apportioning method is still a draft, and may only cover real property and assets without a quoted market price.
Exemptions from the minimum tax for testamentary trusts, deceased estates and special disability trusts are in the Tax Reform No. 3 Bill, which is not law yet.
Some edge cases, such as part-year residents and managed funds or ETFs that are attribution trusts, depend on bills still before Parliament.
